statement: In triangle $ABC$, the bisectors of the angles at $B$ and $C$ meet at the point $I$. Angle $BIC$ is exactly three times as large as angle $BAC$. What is the size of angle $BAC$?

choices.misconception: I used angle $BIC = 90^\circ + \angle BAC$, forgetting that only half of angles $B$ and $C$ are in triangle $BIC$.
I found that the half-angles at $B$ and $C$ add up to $72^\circ$ and gave that.
I found angle $BIC$ and gave that instead of angle $BAC$.
I found the sum of the angles at $B$ and $C$ and gave that.

hints: Triangle $BIC$ contains half of angle $B$ and half of angle $C$. Use the angle sum in triangle $ABC$ to write angle $BIC$ in terms of angle $A$, then set it equal to three times angle $A$.

solutions.reliable: Let angle $BAC = x$. Then $\angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ - x$. In triangle $BIC$ the angles at $B$ and $C$ are half of these, so $\angle BIC = 180^\circ - \frac{1}{2}(180^\circ - x) = 90^\circ + \frac{x}{2}$. Setting $90^\circ + \frac{x}{2} = 3x$ gives $\frac{5x}{2} = 90^\circ$, so $x = 36^\circ$. Check: $\angle BIC = 108^\circ = 3 \times 36^\circ$. The transferable idea: in an angle chase, name one angle and push the triangle angle sum through each triangle in turn.

whyOnTest: Two triangle angle sums, one inside the other, link angle $BIC$ to angle $A$; the common slip is forgetting the halves.
